meta.title: Who really said “Education Is What Remains After You Have Forgotten Everything You Learned In School”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Einstein wrote this sentence in 1936 — while crediting it to an unnamed ‘wit’. The saying is older than him and its author is unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘Education Is What Remains After You Have Forgotten Everything You Learned In School’?
meta.ogDescription: Einstein used the line in 1936 but credited an unnamed ‘wit’. Versions run back to 1892; the real author is anonymous.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — he was quoting an unnamed ‘wit’
answer.sourceLine: Einstein did put this sentence on paper, in the 1936 essay On Education, but he explicitly presented it as someone else’s: “Thus the wit was not wrong who defined education in this way.” Close variants were circulating in American education journals from 1892, decades before Einstein used one, and no one has ever identified who wrote the original.

source.heading: Where Einstein actually used it
source.excerpt: If a young man has trained his muscles and physical endurance by gymnastics and walking, he will later be fitted for every physical work. This is also analogous to the training of the mind and the exercising of the mental and manual skill. Thus the wit was not wrong who defined education in this way: “Education is that which remains, if one has forgotten everything he learned in school.”
trail: Quote Investigator quotes the passage from Einstein’s essay On Education — written in German in 1936, published in English in Out of My Later Years — showing that Einstein ascribed the words to an unidentified ‘wit’. Read the investigation ↗

Wikiquote reaches the same conclusion independently, noting that Einstein ‘did write this quote in “On Education” from 1936 … but it was not his own original quip, he attributed it to an unnamed “wit”’. Wikiquote: Albert Einstein ↗

Quote Investigator dates close precursors to 1892, in an article by C. F. Thwing, president of Western Reserve University, and to 1899 — both well before Einstein used the line. The 1892 and 1899 citations ↗

Quote Investigator’s conclusion is explicit: the family of sayings ‘has an anonymous origin’, and Einstein, B. F. Skinner and the others who used it all declined to claim authorship. QI’s conclusion ↗
source.excerptNote: Einstein’s own framing — he attributes the definition to an unidentified ‘wit’ rather than claiming it.

author.metaLine: Anonymous · earliest close versions in American education journals, 1892–1907
author.bio: Nobody has ever identified the author of this line. The earliest close versions Quote Investigator has traced appear in American education journals in 1892 and 1899, and the first strong matches in December 1907 — one crediting an unnamed college president, the other crediting Ralph Waldo Emerson without support. Everyone famous who has used it since, Einstein and B. F. Skinner included, has attributed it to somebody else.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: An unusual case: the famous name attached to this line actually did write it down — and said in the same breath that it was not his.

items.why: Einstein used the sentence in On Education (1936) but prefaced it with ‘the wit was not wrong who defined education in this way’. He was quoting, and said so. Quote Investigator ↗
A December 1907 issue of The Education Times pinned an early version on Emerson, who had died in 1882. Quote Investigator found no substantive support for the linkage. The 1907 citation ↗

Viscount Halifax, the British ambassador to Washington, used the saying in a 1942 speech and credited ‘a wise man’. Quote Investigator believes it was later reassigned to the 17th-century Marquess of Halifax simply through confusion between the two titles. How the mix-up happened ↗
Skinner used an instance in a 1965 article on teaching and, like Einstein, declined credit for it. The 1965 citation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote it. Quote Investigator finds versions in print from 1892 and concludes the origin is anonymous. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The saying grew out of a real argument in American education journals of the 1890s about what schooling is actually for — whether the point is the facts a student can recite, or the habits of mind left behind once the facts have gone. Writers kept reaching for the same formula, and none of them signed it.

Einstein picked it up because it fitted his own view that training the mind is like training the body: the specific exercise is forgotten, the capacity remains. That he bothered to credit an anonymous wit, and was then credited himself for the next ninety years, is the small irony at the centre of this page.
context.pull: He quoted it, credited someone else, and got the credit anyway.
